rationale: The scrollbar literally exists if and only if the document overflows the viewport — the same condition Newman gave the zip: a field too large to be taken in at once. The mechanism enacts the argument with unusual tightness (P1) and the dual reading is clean: a bold red page with a fat bar for the casual eye, Newman's standing-close instruction and the sublime-as-overflow for the literate one (P7). It fills a gap the motivation correctly identifies in this DNA's chrome-as-material line (favicon, fullscreen, print, color picker) by claiming the one widget they left. Restraint is exemplary — no images, no fonts, no network, one readout, a Mac/touch overlay fallback; the joke lands dry ('the most transcendent line in postwar painting turns out to have been a scroll affordance the whole time, and it still works').
reservations: The scrollbar-as-art gesture has precedent outside this DNA; the specific Newman↔CSS-overflow match is what earns its novelty here, but a stronger anchor (e.g., showing Newman's standing-close instruction translates into the scroll gesture itself, rather than just stating it) would push novelty higher. The synthetic-zip fallback duplicates the native one rather than reinterpreting it — fine, but slightly utilitarian.
revision_suggestion: Consider binding the overlay-fallback zip's drag-handle height more visibly to scroll velocity or dwell, so the 'stand close / grab the zip' instruction has a kinesthetic payoff on touch devices where the native scrollbar is hidden; and surface Newman's actual standing-close quote in the wall label more prominently to sharpen the double-coding.
